newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DSM H1 net up 13 pct, upbeat on 1997.
newsitem.headline: DSM H1 net up 13 pct, upbeat on 1997.

text.p: Dutch chemicals group DSM NV on Wednesday reported first-half net profits up 13 percent at 465 million guilders and said it saw clearly higher full-year earnings.
"This summer, demand is good, prices are good, margins are good...our competitive position in the world remains strong," board member Loek Ligthart told a results news conference.
Turnover increased 18 percent year-on-year to 6.12 billion guilders, with volumes accounting for 11 percent of the rise, sales prices four percent and currencies three percent.
Ligthart said he expected the first-half profit upturn to continue at the same rate in the second half, but declined to detail prospects further ahead.
"We don't have any specific figures to offer for 1998/1999," he said.

Higher raw material prices in the first half of 1997, coupled with increased fixed costs due to acquisitions and expansions, resulted in slightly lower margins (sales price per tonne minus variable costs) year-on-year, Ligthart said.

Operating profits in industrial and fine chemicals fell to 183 million guilders from 314 million in the year-ago period, with business dampened by maintenance shutdowns in caprolactam and melamine and a fall in fertilizers.
Ligthart said higher gas prices -- the raw material for fertilizers -- had pressured margins, but added he expected these to come down in line with oil prices.
Fine chemicals showed a "considerable increase" in both sales and operating profits, mainly due to acquisitions, higher selling prices and the strong dollar, DSM said.
Operating profits at the polymers and performance materials division mushroomed to 264 million guilders from 72 a year earlier, as margins for hydrocarbons and polyethylene improved.
However margins for other products fell on higher raw material prices, Ligthart said.
He said DSM's recent Gelsenkirchen buy represented an investment of some one thousand guilders per tonne in expanding polyolefin (polyethylene and polypropylene) production.
"That is very, very competitive," he said.
DSM announced last week it had allocated a total of one billion guilders until the year 2000 for acquiring and expanding the Vestolen plant in Gelsenkirchen, Germany.
Ligthart said there had been no change in DSM's strategy of focusing equally on all its businesses and to be the best of class in all of them.
He said DSM was satisfied with its current growth rate, and that -- if possible -- the company would prefer to expand in Asia and the U.S.
"But in Asia, firms belong to parties who won't sell. You have to gradually build a position, which is what we are doing at this moment," he said, adding prices for U.S. firms had risen considerably.
All divisions had ample opportunity to expand provided candidates met DSM's profitability criteria, he said.
Returns on investment had to amount to some 15 percent or at least exceed the weighted average cost of capital.
This held true both for prospective acquisitions and existing businesses, he said.

"As long as we think (business units) are performing well in the longer term and making a good average return, they belong to the club. If we think they don't have that potential...(they're) up for sale in principle.
DSM shares were down 13.10 guilders to 216.90 guilders at 1140 GMT, near their session-low of 215.50 guilders.
